Sleep Problems

night events · insomnia · sleep apnea · narcolepsy · restless legs · circadianEarly or late in the night, and is the trouble sleeping or staying awake?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Usually early, unresponsive, no memory NREM (non-rapid eye movement) arousal: sleep terror, sleepwalking; mostly late, alert, recalls a dream nightmare
  • Snoring in a child polysomnography; in an adult polysomnography or a home test
  • Insomnia behavioral treatment first: sleep training in a child, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for insomnia in an adult
What it is

Cycles of about 90 minutes, 4 to 6 a night light NREM, deep NREM (N3) and REM (rapid eye movement) Share of the nightShares of sleep, each about: N1 5%, N2 45%, N3 25%, REM 25%

Deep sleep early; REM periods lengthen toward morning

Driver

Deep NREM incomplete arousal: sleep terrors, sleepwalking

REM: dreaming muscles atonic except the eyes and diaphragm

Chain

Usually the first half, NREM confused or terrified, may sweat with a fast pulse, unresponsive no memory

Mostly the second half, REM nightmare wakes oriented, recalls the dream

REM without atonia dream enactment: REM sleep behavior disorder

Insights

Atonia keeps the dream still lose it and the dream is acted out, not just recalled

Narcolepsy is thought to be hypocretin deficiency hypocretin-1 is low in spinal fluid in type 1

2Urgent risks
SeizureRepetitive, stereotyped behaviors or posturing at night

If night events are stereotyped and repetitive, choose a nocturnal seizure workup.

InjuryActing out dreams, often an older man
Strongly linked to Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, multiple system atrophy May be drug-induced: common on antidepressants

If dreams are acted out, choose a safer bedroom (bed lowered toward the floor) and video polysomnography.

ChildSnoring with attention problems
Screen for snoring at every well-child visit Peak 2 to 8 years: big tonsils and adenoids
AdultLoud snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness
Complications include hypertension and atrial fibrillation
3Differential
Events in the night, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Sleep terrorsSits up screaming; no memoryUsually the first half, most often the first third; terror with an autonomic surge, not comforted Most common at ages 3 to 7
NightmaresFrightening dreamMostly the second half; wakes oriented and alert; recalls the dream
Confusional arousalsEyes open or closed; no memoryUsually the first half; confused in bed, resists waking
SleepwalkingIncomplete arousal from NREM; no memoryUsually the earlier third of the night; leaves the bed
Nocturnal seizuresPosturing at nightRepetitive and stereotyped
REM sleep behavior disorderActs out dreamsREM, mostly later in the night; REM without atonia on video study Older man
Poor sleep or sleepy by day, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Behavioral insomnia (sleep-onset association)Bedtime problems and night wakingsFalls asleep only with set conditions or actions from a parent Healthy child
Chronic insomniaTrouble falling or staying asleep, early waking or unrefreshing sleep3 or more times a week for 3 months or more
Obstructive sleep apnea, childSnoring, attention problemsPeaks at 2 to 8 years with big tonsils and adenoids
Obstructive sleep apnea, adultLoud snoring; obesity, male sex, older ageWitnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness; polysomnography or a home test confirms
NarcolepsySleepy by day; sleep paralysis; hallucinations as sleep starts or endsChronic; cataplexy: brief weakness, awake, set off by sudden emotion such as laughter
Delayed sleep phaseAsleep and up late (eg 3 AM to 10 AM)Normal sleep on their own schedule Teen
Restless legs syndromeUrge to move the legs, with unpleasant sensationsWorse in the evening and at night; eased by moving
Early-morning waking2 weeks or more of low mood or loss of interest; then REM sooner, less deep sleep
Advanced sleep phaseWakes very earlyAlso goes to bed early Older adult
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Late in the night, alert, tells the dreamNightmare, not a sleep terrorAsk about trauma and mood
Child snores and cannot pay attentionObstructive sleep apneaPolysomnography
Brief weakness while awake, set off by laughter, in a sleepy patientCataplexy: narcolepsySleep study, then daytime nap test
Leg urge in pregnancy or end-stage kidney diseaseRestless legs syndromeIron studies
Teen cannot fall asleep before 3 AM but sleeps well when allowedDelayed sleep phaseProgressively earlier rising with morning bright light

Pause point. The bait: a sleep study or EEG (electroencephalography) for a classic sleep terror, or a stimulant for a snoring child. Polysomnography is for suspected apnea, dream enactment or narcolepsy, not a classic sleep terror; a seizure workup is for stereotyped movements; a child who snores with poor attention needs the study first.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: chronic insomnia Symptom – trouble falling or staying asleep, or early waking · Frequency – 3 or more times a week · Duration – 3 months or more
Defining tests: narcolepsy Symptom – chronic daytime sleepiness, often with cataplexy · Latency – average time to fall asleep 8 minutes or less on daytime naps · REM – REM at sleep onset in 2 or more of 5 naps
Defining criteria: REM sleep behavior disorder Behavior – dream enactment · Study – REM sleep without atonia on in-lab video polysomnography
6Severity
Adult obstructive sleep apnea: apnea-hypopnea index (events per hour of sleep)
SeverityEvents per hour
Mild5 to 15
ModerateMore than 15 to 30
SevereMore than 30
7Treatment
Treat by problem
ProblemFirstThen or watch for
Sleep terrorsReassure and educate; keep the child safe; more total sleepNever shorten sleep
SleepwalkingLock windows and outer doors; remove breakable objects–
NightmaresCBT; adult with PTSD (posttraumatic stress disorder): image rehearsal therapyPrazosin may be used for PTSD nightmares; in a child, ask about trauma and mood
Behavioral insomnia of childhoodBehavioral interventionsNo hypnotics
Obstructive sleep apnea, childAdenotonsillectomyDiagnose by polysomnography first
Obstructive sleep apnea, adultCPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), the most effective; weight loss if overweightWeight loss alone is usually not curative
Chronic insomnia, adultCBT for insomnia What it includesCognitive restructuring, stimulus control, sleep hygiene, relaxation, and sleep restriction, the most effective partOlder adult: no benzodiazepine or other sedative-hypnotic as the first choice
NarcolepsyModafinil; an oxybate also treats cataplexy; brief naps at set timesNaps under 30 minutes
REM sleep behavior disorderBedroom safety plus melatonin, clonazepam or pramipexoleAsk about antidepressants
Restless legs syndromeIron if stores are low (step 4); gabapentin or pregabalin firstDopamine agonists no longer standard: symptoms worsen with long use (augmentation)
Delayed sleep phaseProgressively earlier rising with morning bright lightPerhaps melatonin 4 to 5 hours before the desired bedtime
Advanced sleep phaseBright light in the eveningLight-blocking goggles in the morning
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Sleep terrors continue despite reassurance and safetyScheduled awakenings, shortly before the usual episode time
Chronic insomnia not better with CBT for insomniaMedication may be considered, short term Watch forBenzodiazepines: dependence. Z-drugs: car crashes, falls, fractures. Antihistamines: little evidence.
Narcolepsy not helped by, or intolerant of, wake-promoting drugsMethylphenidate or an amphetamine
Restless legs in pregnancyExpect relief within weeks of delivery
REM sleep behavior disorderMany later develop Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia or multiple system atrophy (about 74% by 12 years): watch for new neurologic signs
Practice
  1. 6-year-old boy wakes crying most nights in the early morning hours tells his parents a dog was chasing him; settles after a hug happy and busy by day T 36.8 °C · examination normal · no snoring → Nightmares → late in the night, fully awake, recalls the dream and can be comforted: REM nightmares; sleep terrors and confusional arousals come early from NREM sleep with no memory
  2. 4-year-old girl sits up screaming about 90 minutes after falling asleep sweaty and breathing fast; does not respond as her parents try to comfort her no memory of it next morning HR 150/min during an episode · daytime examination normal → Sleep terrors → usually early in the night, autonomic arousal, unresponsive to comfort and amnesia: NREM sleep terrors; nightmares come late with recall, and seizures are stereotyped and repetitive
  3. 5-year-old boy with screaming episodes 1 to 2 hours after bedtime, twice a week inconsolable for minutes, then sleeps; remembers nothing no snoring, no jerking or stiffening afebrile · neurologic examination normal → Reassure and keep him safe → classic sleep terrors at a typical age: reassure, educate and ensure safety; snoring would call for a sleep study and repetitive stereotyped movements for a seizure workup
  4. 6-year-old girl screams, unconsolable, nightly at about 10:30 pm for 2 months parents have reassured her and made the room safe she still has episodes most nights afebrile · no snoring · examination normal → Wake her before the usual time → scheduled awakenings, before the expected episode, are a listed treatment; total sleep should be increased, not shortened; polysomnography is for suspected obstructive sleep apnea, and she does not snore
  5. 5-year-old boy snores loudly every night with pauses and gasps teacher reports poor attention; restless sleep, wakes tired BMI (body mass index) 50th percentile · tonsils nearly touching · BP 98/60 mm Hg → Polysomnography → snoring with attention problems and big tonsils suggests obstructive sleep apnea; polysomnography is required to make the diagnosis, and adenotonsillectomy is first-line treatment; attention problems are a listed feature of the apnea, so test for it before a stimulant
  6. 2-year-old boy will not fall asleep unless a parent lies beside him wakes twice a night and needs the same to fall back asleep healthy, growing well T 36.7 °C · examination normal · no snoring → Behavioral sleep training → sleep-onset association insomnia: behavioral interventions are first-line, and hypnotics are not recommended for behavioral insomnia; with no snoring, polysomnography is not indicated
  7. 9-year-old boy found walking in the dark kitchen an hour after bedtime eyes open, mumbling; back in bed without waking; no memory twice this month afebrile · examination normal · no snoring → Secure doors and windows → sleepwalking is an NREM arousal, usually in the first half of the night; safety measures such as locking windows and outer doors reduce injury; with no snoring or stereotyped movements, neither a sleep study nor a seizure workup is indicated
Pairs with Tics and Tic Disorders: at night, repetitive stereotyped behaviors or posturing call for a nocturnal seizure workup
Transferable rule

Early in the night with no memory usually means a NREM arousal; late, awake and recalling a dream is a nightmare.
